source_boundary.preserved_question_intent: Explain the relationship and practical differences between Spring Framework and Spring Boot, especially Spring's core container/programming model versus Boot's starters, auto-configuration, application running and production-ready conveniences, without treating them as mutually exclusive replacements.

sources.title: Spring Framework Reference — Introduction to the Spring IoC Container and Beans
anchors: Spring Framework implements IoC and dependency injection through its container
org.springframework.beans and org.springframework.context form the basis of the IoC container

sources.title: Spring Boot — Project Overview
anchors: Spring Boot creates stand-alone production-grade Spring-based applications
Boot takes an opinionated view of the Spring platform and third-party libraries
Boot provides embedded server options, starter dependencies, auto-configuration, externalized configuration and production-ready features

sources.title: Spring Boot Reference — Auto-configuration
anchors: auto-configuration attempts to configure a Spring application based on jar dependencies
auto-configuration is non-invasive and user configuration can replace specific defaults
specific auto-configuration classes can be excluded

sources.title: Spring Boot Reference — Build Systems / Starters
anchors: starters provide a supported set of managed transitive dependencies for common application capabilities

sources.title: Spring Boot Reference — Production-ready Features
anchors: Spring Boot provides additional features for monitoring and managing applications in production
auditing, health and metrics can be exposed through production-ready features

claims.text: Spring Boot is for building Spring-based applications; it does not replace Spring Framework. Spring Framework supplies foundational container/programming-model capabilities while Boot reduces application assembly and operational setup.
Spring Framework's core container implements IoC/DI and is the foundation on which Spring applications compose managed beans and dependencies.

Spring Boot adds opinionated application conventions and common application conveniences such as starters, auto-configuration, executable/embedded-server application patterns, externalized configuration and production-ready features.
Boot auto-configuration is conditional and non-invasive: it attempts defaults based on application conditions, can back off when user configuration is supplied, and can be explicitly excluded.
Starters primarily package convenient dependency descriptors and managed transitive dependency sets; they are not the same responsibility as auto-configuration.

writer_constraints: Treat Spring Framework and Spring Boot as layered/complementary, not mutually exclusive alternatives.
Lead with Spring Framework IoC/DI and core framework capabilities, then explain Boot's application assembly/runtime conveniences.
Keep Starter and auto-configuration responsibilities distinct.
Describe auto-configuration as conditional/non-invasive and mention user overrides/exclusions; do not call it opaque magic.
Do not claim Spring Framework requires XML while Boot uniquely enables annotations or Java configuration.
Do not claim Boot is inherently faster at runtime; distinguish developer/setup convenience from application performance.
Do not equate Actuator with a complete production operations platform.
Do not fabricate project migrations, performance gains or production incidents.
